newsitem.title: USA: Texas police deploy close to armed separatists.
newsitem.headline: Texas police deploy close to armed separatists.

text.p: Elite police units moved within striking distance late on Friday of armed Texas separatists holed up in a mountain compound and officials said the rebels were preparing for a shootout.

The deployment signalled that police patience with the six-day standoff may be running out and struck panic in the self- styled Republic of Texas group, whose leader called out for help on shortwave radio: "Mayday, mayday, mayday, hostiles invading Republic of Texas embassy. This is a mayday call to any nation of the world."

Texas Department of Public Safety spokesman Mike Cox told reporters the rebels hiding out in the west Texas mountains had been ordered to open fire on the advancing police units although no shots had been fired.
Cox said one Republic member was heard over a radio frequency ordering others to "fire at will" and "put the laser on him (a police officer) and pluck him."

He described the advance of Special Weapons and Tactics Teams (SWAT) as a "major tactical operation where substantial ground was covered" and that the units were within 440 yards (metres) of the compound where Republic leader Richard McLaren and six followers were hiding.

Police, who had been deployed two miles away, were ordered to advance after minimal progress in negotiations aimed at coaxing McLaren and the other separatists, who believe Texas is an independent nation, to surrender.
Cox refused to say if or when police planned to raid the compound, but said they had "bent over backwards" to accommodate McLaren's demands with little to show for it.
"We have tried everything we can think of to be cooperative with McLaren. This is a matter that needs to be resolved in a courtroom, not out here in the Davis Mountains," he said.
But McLaren, a 43-year-old vintner from Missouri, was defiant. In the shortwave radio tape, aired on a Houston television station, McLaren told police, "We'll take a good hunk of you boys with us."

Estimates of up to 200 heavily armed police have surrounded the rebel base since the siege began on Sunday when the Republic group seized two hostages in retaliation for the arrest of its security chief, Robert Scheidt.

The hostages were later released in exchange for Scheidt, who on Friday became the first rebel to walk out of the ramshackle compound McLaren calls "the embassy" and surrender to police. Felony charges for the kidnapping were filed against six of the Republicans.

The Republic of Texas, which formed in 1995 and has ties to militias, says the 1845 annexation of Texas by the United States was illegal. Texas was an independent nation for nine years after breaking away from Mexico in 1836 in a rebellion that McLaren likens to his own.

"Everyone has chosen to stay and hold the sovereign soil of the Republic and its foreign missions...I pray reinforcements arrive before they overrun the embassy," he said in a letter that bore overtones of a famous missive sent out by Col. William Barrett Travis, commander of the forces at the Alamo in Texas' war for independence from Mexico.
All 187 Alamo defenders, including Travis, died when the Mexican army attacked after a 13-day siege.
Cox, who read the letter to reporters, said five of the seven rebels in the compound, including McLaren, had sent out wills, underscoring their determination to fight to the death.

Adding urgency to the police desire to end the standoff is the fear that it may become yet another rallying point for anti-government militias. At least nine armed men have been arrested this week moving toward the rebel position.

Terence O'Rourke, attorney for McLaren, said he had asked Texas Gov. George W. Bush to stop the police from moving in to give him more time to negotiate a peaceful end. But a Bush spokeswoman said he would not intervene.
